entries.title: Sununu to Face Pappas in New Hampshire Senate Race
entries.summary: The Republican and Democrat won their respective primaries to square off in November.
entries.content:
By HOLLY RAMER and KATHY McCORMACK

CONCORD, N.H. — New Hampshire primary voters chose candidates for Congress, governor and the 424-seat state Legislature on Tuesday, and incumbents weren’t the only familiar names on the ballot.

Former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu, a Republican, will face Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas in November in the race to replace U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, whose decision to not seek reelection created a cascade of competitive races.

Two of the eight Republicans hoping to replace the three-term Democrat were former U.S. senators she previously defeated: Sununu and Scott Brown. Pappas, whose departure from his 1st Congressional District seat in turn attracted a crowd of candidates, defeated four candidates in the Democratic primary for the open Senate seat.

Shaheen’s daughter, Stefany Shaheen, was among those seeking the Democratic nomination for Pappas’ seat, along with former candidate Maura Sullivan. Several other candidates in top races also were making repeat appearances.

Anthony DiLorenzo won the Republican primary in the 1st District, while Lily Tang Williams won the GOP primary in the 2nd. She’ll face U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander, a Democrat seeking a second term.

Ex-GOP senators sought a return to Congress, while House member wants promotion

Sununu, who spent six years in the U.S. House and one term in the Senate before being ousted by Shaheen in 2008, has this time focused on themes including affordability for housing, healthcare and energy, holding Congress accountable and constituent service.

“I’ve been out of politics for 17 years. I’m not worried about reelection,” he said during a campaign stop last month. “I don’t need an appointment or a job. I don’t need to make anyone happy. I need to do one thing: Stand up for the people of New Hampshire.”

Brown previously represented Massachusetts, where he won a special election in 2010 after the death of Sen. Ted Kennedy before losing in 2012. He unsuccessfully challenged Shaheen in 2014 and served as ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa during President Donald Trump’s first term.

In a July interview, he said he decided to run again because New Hampshire Republicans have no representation in Congress and because, in his view, his experience as a veteran, lawmaker, ambassador and grandfather is unmatched.

He accuses Sununu — whose father and younger brother are former governors — of coasting on his name. Sununu also has the backing of Trump, despite having called him “a loser” in 2024, but Brown said that will just make him beholden to the president and other special interests.

“I’m the only truly independent candidate here who can actually vote on anything with a clear conscience and with New Hampshire’s best interests at heart,” Brown said.

Jim Loomis, 83, of Bow, said he backed Brown in 2014 but not on Tuesday because “he never got traction back again.” He acknowledged Sununu had been out of politics for even longer but still voted for him.

“I think what he’s done for work over the years has kept him close enough to what’s going on, and then with his family ties, I just think he’s got a more stable base,” he said.

Pappas, who is giving up his House seat after four terms, raised twice as much money as Sununu and Brown combined and dwarfed his Democratic primary opponents, as well. He also enjoyed a wide lead in polls, though recently lost some ground to scientist and democratic socialist Karishma Manzur.

Kristin Selesnick, 41, of Bow, said Pappas was a “fine” candidate but she doesn’t like that he accepts money from super PACs and that he voted “present” on a measure to restrict weapons sales to Israel instead of voting no. She voted for Manzur.

“I just like her whole platform,” she said. “I think she would be a great voice for the Granite State.”

Open seat in 1st District attracts a crowd, while 2nd District was quieter

Stefany Shaheen and Sullivan were the leading candidates among seven seeking the Democratic nomination in the 1st District.

Shaheen is a former city councilor in Portsmouth. She founded a business to help people with chronic medical conditions after one of her daughters was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes. She also is part of a bio-tech initiative in New Hampshire to advance regenerative medicine.

Sullivan is a former Marine and Iraq War veteran who served as an assistant secretary at the Department of Veterans Affairs under President Barack Obama. A vice chair of the New Hampshire Democratic Party, Sullivan ran for the 1st District seat in 2018, losing in an 11-candidate primary to Pappas in his first congressional bid.

On the Republican side, political newcomer DiLorenzo, who owns a chain of car dealerships and has been endorsed by Trump, won the Republican primary. He defeated three other candidates, including Hollie Noveletsky, a veteran and nurse practitioner who runs a steel fabrication company and ran for the same seat two years ago.

In the 2nd District, first-term incumbent Goodlander overcame a primary challenge from Paige Beauchemin, a progressive state lawmaker and nurse. Tang Williams, who was the nominee two years ago and was making her third attempt at the seat, won the Republican primary.

Nominations for governor and down ballot races were also at stake

In contrast to the all-Democratic congressional delegation, Republicans dominate state government.

Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte defeated two little-known opponents in her primary as she seeks a second two-year term. Cinde Warmington, a healthcare attorney, was unopposed for the Democratic nomination.

Voters also were nominating candidates for the entire state Legislature, where Republicans hold a roughly 40-vote majority in the 400-member House and outnumber Democrats in the Senate 16-8.

Accustomed to going first when it comes to presidential primaries, New Hampshire is among the last states to hold state-level primary elections, leaving the winners just eight weeks to woo voters before Nov. 3. But legislation passed this year moves future state primaries to the second Tuesday in June.

entries.title: Duffy Scolds Ford Over Deals With China in Urging More American Manufacturing
entries.summary: Ford called the transportation secretary’s letter a “wrongheaded attempt to capture headlines” and said it contains numerous factual errors.
entries.content:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has warned Ford Motor Company about maintaining “questionable foreign alliances” with Chinese companies amid calls from the Trump administration to reshore its manufacturing operations.

In a recent letter to Ford CEO Jim Farley, Duffy derided the company’s recent deals with China-backed auto manufacturers, and said Ford “fails to act as [a] reliable partner” to the American public.

“The company’s recent strategic decisions paint a troubling picture of a foundational American brand actively intertwining its future with Chinese state-backed enterprises,” Duffy wrote in the letter sent Sept. 3 and released publicly Tuesday.

Ford pushed back sharply in a statement to NOTUS on Tuesday, calling Duffy’s letter an error-filled and “wrongheaded attempt to capture headlines.”

The company said it produces more vehicles in the United States and employs more American workers than any other automaker.

Ford has been under continued pressure from the White House to return to domestic supply chains and manufacturing, and recently announced it would relocate manufacturing operations of its Lincoln models from China to the United States by 2030.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick recently celebrated the announcement as a tariff success, but Duffy asserted the four-year timeline “leaves an unacceptable, multi-year window of reliance on Chinese manufacturing while depriving skilled American workers of vital manufacturing jobs.”

Duffy went on to highlight Ford’s dependence on licensed technology from Chinese battery manufacturer Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited — a company that appears on the Defense Department’s list of banned companies. He also criticized Ford over a new deal with Chinese automotive company Geely Auto to build zero-emission vehicles at a Ford factory in Spain.

Ford defended its arrangement with Chinese battery makers, saying its Michigan battery hub is owned and operated by Ford and can’t be classified as a foreign-owned manufacturing operation. The company said Duffy’s assessment of its operations in Spain are also fraught.

“Ford supports the Trump administration’s vision for advancing American innovation and manufacturing,” Ford’s response states. “Had Secretary Duffy reached out before issuing his letter to the press, we would have been happy to share more details about Ford’s U.S. commitment.”

entries.title: Prosecutor Says Man Accused of Charging Ohio Candidate Wanted to Ask Questions
entries.summary: The man had weapons but never brandished them, authorities said.
entries.content:
By JOEY CAPPELLETTI and JAMIE STENGLE

CANFIELD, Ohio — An armed man accused of charging toward Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton during a campaign stop at a fair was trying to ask the Democrat questions, a prosecutor said during the man's arraignment Tuesday.

No one has publicly said what 38-year-old Patrick Havas wanted to ask Acton, but authorities have said he never brandished or unholstered the weapons he had on him and they haven't found any threats in a search of his cellphone. As he charged toward Acton, authorities said, he knocked down two people before troopers stopped him.

Havas pleaded not guilty to two counts of assault, one count of disorderly conduct and one count of inducing panic. His bond was set at $5,000.

He was arrested after authorities said he knocked people down while forcing his way through a crowd Sunday as Acton spoke under a tent at the fair in Canfield in northeastern Ohio. Authorities said he had two handguns, a taser and a set of brass knuckles.

“He appeared in that tent wanting to ask questions,” Mahoning County Prosecutor Lynn Maro told the judge during the hearing. “You should know law enforcement gained consent for them to have complete access to his cellphone so they found no threats.”

Maro said after the hearing that the video Havas took shows him “walking into the tent recording and moving forward, calling out her name.” Acton, a physician, is the state’s former public health director.

“All he got out was Dr. Acton, Dr. Acton,” Maro said.

Maro said that the investigation is continuing, and noted the Mahoning County Sheriff's Office is asking the public for any video capturing what happened.

Acton’s security detail, made up of troopers with the Ohio State Highway Patrol, intercepted Havas as he forced his way through the crowd, the agency has said. A highway patrol spokesman said they did not have any bodycam footage from the incident.

Two people were treated at the scene on Sunday and released, according to an incident report from the Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office.

Mike Ray, a city councilman in Youngstown who is also a member of the Ohio Democratic Party’s executive committee, said he was in a corner behind Acton as she spoke. Then, he said, he could tell that something was going on among those in the crowd facing Acton, and he saw two people who were standing in front of their mobility scooters “tumble to the ground.”

Havas’ attorney, J. Gerald Ingram, said at the hearing that his client has lived with his mother in Canfield for the past 30 years and is not a flight risk.

“He really has nowhere to go,” said Ingram, who declined to make any comments after the hearing.

The Ohio gubernatorial race is one of the most high-profile races this year as the campaigns enter the final six weeks of campaigning before the election in November. Acton is facing Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who has parlayed his national name recognition, tech industry connections and alliance with President Donald Trump into a record fundraising haul. Ramaswamy’s campaign called the incident unacceptable.

The judge on Tuesday ordered that Havas have no contact with Acton or the two people who were knocked down, and that he forfeit any guns. He was also ordered to refrain from speaking with the media.

Addie Bullock, spokesperson for the Acton campaign, said in a statement following the hearing that Acton and her husband were “grateful to see the rule of law upheld,” and extended their “continued appreciation to law enforcement.”

Former U.S. Rep. John Boccieri, a Democratic candidate for the Ohio House, said he was near Acton in the tent when Havas “came in very aggressively” with his cellphone in the air screaming Acton’s name while rushing toward her. He said officers quickly “sprang into action,” grabbed the man and pulled him out of the tent.

Boccieri said he immediately jumped forward to make sure Acton was OK, which she was. And, he said, she’d already started helping a man who was face down in the mud after being knocked down.

___

Stengle contributed to this report from Dallas.

entries.title: Welcome to The Washington Sun
entries.content:
Washington journalism is in a moment of generational change. We’re rising to meet it.

Welcome to The Washington Sun.

We launched two years ago as NOTUS, a news site focused on national politics and policy. But as we watched others pull back on Washington coverage, we knew our hometown deserved better. So we invested — more than doubling the size of our newsroom in just six months.

We’ve added local reporting from Martin Austermuhle, Jenny Gathright, Michael Brice-Saddler, Zara Norman and Shamira Muhammad, columns from Dana Milbank, Matt K. Lewis and Thomas Boswell, food coverage from Tom Sietsema and weather forecasts from what used to be called the Capital Weather Gang. We hired Paul Kane and Kadia Goba to join the best congressional reporting team in D.C., Jeff Stein to cover economic policy, and Elena Schneider on politics. We’ve added reporters to cover federal agencies and law enforcement, we’re building out our teams for breaking news and features, and we now have more staff reporters covering local sports than anyone else in the DMV.

Our work puts Washington front and center, and we wanted our name to do the same. So NOTUS — short for News of the United States — is now The Washington Sun.

Why The Sun? You can choose your metaphor: We’re shining a light on Washington. Everything is clearer in daylight. And we’d rather light a big candle than keep on cursing the darkness.

We cover politics and policy and the people who shape life in Washington — not just at the White House and in Congress, but at the Wilson Building, at Northwest Stadium and in the neighborhoods where we live.

We report for the people who live here, the people who make policy here, and the people around the world who care deeply about what happens here. We do it with original reporting, with deep sourcing and with an unwavering commitment to accuracy.

And we do it with a newsroom unlike any other in Washington, bringing together veteran journalists and some of the country’s most promising up-and-coming reporters — individuals from different regions, backgrounds and beliefs who have come to D.C. as fellows at the Allbritton Journalism Institute.

We’ve got the financial backing of Robert Allbritton, the founding publisher of POLITICO. We’re supported by advertisers who buy ads on our website and sponsor our newsletters, podcasts and events — and by paid subscriptions from readers who value what we do. We’re grateful to everyone who makes our work possible, but our editorial decisions are entirely our own.

If you’ve got tips, story ideas or thoughts on our coverage, reach out to us at newsroom@washsun.com. For advertising, please contact partnerships@washsun.com.

If you’re interested in working for The Sun, write to us at jobs@washsun.com.

We’d love to hear from you.

entries.title: The Nats, the Blown Saves Record, and Unforeseen Expectations
entries.summary: The Nationals have blown more saves than any team in MLB history. But there's more to it than just an embarrassing record.
entries.content:
For the Nationals, unwanted history looked a lot like the slow and painful march to it. When the eighth inning began in San Diego on Tuesday night, they had a three-run lead. When it ended, they trailed by a run in an eventual 5-4 loss to the Padres. In between, they blew a save for the 38th time this season, an MLB record that speaks for itself, both loudly and plainly.

This bullpen has not been good at doing the basic job of a bullpen, which is to take leads at some point in the middle to late inning and ferry them into the win column. And this blown save, like many before it, was a team effort, starting when Jared Simpson, a 26-year-old lefty, walked the bases loaded with no outs. Those were the only three batters he faced. Behind him, Erik Tolman, a 27-year-old lefty, allowed a sacrifice fly, then a soft single up the middle — a hit that floated just past his glove — that brought in the two runs that tied the score.

That was No. 38, which felt all too predictable once Simpson couldn’t find the strike zone. How the Nats got here … well, you lived it. There was that eight-run lead that evaporated in San Francisco. There were those crushing games against the Phillies in June, back when the season still had juice. Then, fatefully, there was Tuesday night. The relievers for the 2024 White Sox, the team that lost the most games in modern history, are officially off the hook. Tolman, Clatyon Beeter, Mitchell Parker, Orlando Ribalta, Richard Lovelady, Tom Cosgrove, Brad Lord, Cole Henry, Yovanny Cruz, PJ Poulin, Gus Varland, Matt Krook, Ken Waldichuk, Riley Cornelio, Paxton Schultz and Max Kranick have the watch now.

That’s every reliever who’s blown a save for Washington this season. There are, of course, other ways to illustrate what this Nationals season has dissolved into. After the loss to the Padres on Tuesday, the Nats have dropped six in a row. They have also lost 20 of their last 22 road games. The blown saves, though, have become the billboard for everything wrong with the Nationals in 2026. I get it, too, given that it’s a stat that shows how often a glaring team weakness has directly contributed to losses.

But the blown saves are not a 2-D story, no matter how simple it’s felt whenever the thin wall between dread and hope has collapsed. Case in point: Now that the Nationals have set the record, it will be tempting to refer to their bullpen as historically bad. But as it stands, their bullpen ERA — 5.09 through Tuesday— is a half run better than where it settled last season (5.59). The 2025 team, however, finished with just 20 blown saves, which was mostly because it had far fewer leads to protect. And this is where the emotional calculus of this year’s pen gets a third dimension, if not a fourth and fifth.

It was immediately clear that in the first year under Paul Toboni, the club’s new president of baseball operations, the bats were way, way ahead of the arms. The blown saves have been the most on-the-nose example of that. They’ve also shown how the Nats’ early, unexpected success has warped the experience of following a team that wasn’t initially penciled in for so many late leads.

In spite of trades and recent injuries to key hitters, the Nationals’ offense still ranks second in runs and homers, a contrast to the team’s record of 67-80. The bullpen, then, has been the heaviest counterweight while pitching the second-most relief innings in the league. Between personnel decisions, in-game strategy and player development, dissecting the team’s pitching process should be a major focus of the offseason, which is to say nothing of the need to spend more across the roster, not just on relievers, to compete more in 2027.

But in the moment, the blown saves feel, at least in part, like a wonky blip of an interrupted growth curve. It was as if the Nats were gifted a fancy grill — stick with me, that’s the offense — while living in an apartment with no outdoor space. (Ownership choosing to live in said apartment for another year is a story for a different day.)

None of that’s to say this Nats bullpen is misunderstood or something. It is perfectly understood as downright abysmal. And what’s that prescient George Orwell bit from 1984? The one that goes … “The Party told you to reject the evidence of your eyes and ears. It was their final, most essential command.” A bit heavy-handed for baseball, maybe, but the point is it’s just not what we’re doing here. That is someone else’s job.

But if the blown saves are to explain what ultimately felled the Nationals’ season, it feels useful — important, even — to point out how so many happened. The biggest reason is that the team’s relievers have struggled with two central goals of pitching: throwing strikes and limiting hard contact. A close second, though, is all those leads existing in the first place. Again, taken together, it’s another way to describe how the first four months of 2026 could shape the entire public perception of the Toboni-Blake Butera era (or at least the start of it). The team wasn’t built to win, then the offense raked enough to hang on the edge of the playoff race through mid-July. But because it wasn’t built to win, the Nats spent no money on the bullpen over the winter, which slowed the whole thing down until the wheels fell off.

If, as a fan, you knew a season was lost from the beginning — if that were somehow a guarantee — you might sign up for a lower bullpen ERA with a higher number of blown saves. The latter, you might figure, would be arbitrary in the grand scheme. But a lower ERA, even by half a run, would maybe portend better for future years, when your team finally spends on its roster again. (That’s just never a guarantee, either, which you know if you live in D.C.)

This summer, though, because of James Wood, CJ Abrams, Luis García Jr. and Curtis Mead, among others, rational and dispassionate started mixing with emotional and reactionary. That’s never not tricky for a fan base, especially when it comes ahead of schedule. If you live in D.C., you also know that to be true now. Because on one hand, many of the rotating bullpen arms, guys like Krook, Kranick and Cosgrove, were always more likely to be trivia answers than actual solutions. This was by design, too, at least in the sense that the front office didn’t expect to have one of the league’s best offenses. But once that offense kept mashing, the blown saves were the worst possible outcome, no matter if another form of torture would have painted an even bleaker statistical picture.

The real question, then, has little to do with blown saves or ERA or (fill in your advanced pitching analytic of choice). It’s whether a problem born of unforeseen expectations is better or worse than having no immediate problems at all.

Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Sept. 9, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

What was once NOTUS is now The Washington Sun! While the name may have changed, what remains the same is our commitment to covering the District the way it deserves to be covered. That means sports stories from Northwest Stadium to high school gyms; local politics coverage from the streets of D.C. to the halls of the Wilson Building; food writing from Tom Sietsema; an eye on the sky from Capital Weather; and the kind of entertaining, illuminating coverage you can’t find anywhere else. We’re excited to have you along for the ride.

In today’s newsletter: A trip to D.C.’s lost and found, the best meals under $25 and Thomas Boswell on Jayden Daniels. 

Today’s Daily Digit: 6/10. Some spots have a shot at 90 degrees. But September heat isn't as harsh as midsummer, and humidity is still relatively tame. Full forecast from Capital Weather.





THE LATEST

D.C. has its own municipal lost and found, and we got a peek inside. A D.C. office known as the Unclaimed Property Unit serves as the city’s official depository of people’s lost stuff, collecting everything from millions of dollars worth of misdelivered checks to family heirlooms left in forgotten safe-deposit boxes.

As The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports, the unit’s staff collects and catalogues what it can, auctioning off items such as rare coins and jewelry while endeavoring to reunite personal belongings with their owners. And yes, sometimes they find strange things: gold teeth, locks of hair, a diaper and even state secrets.

“We get teeth all the time,” one worker told us, sounding none too pleased.





DEEP DIVE

DC0A3355 copy.jpg (8192x5462, AR: 1.50)
It can be hard to find good food on a budget. Tom Sietsema, The Sun’s food correspondent, believes that the best values come from restaurants where “the experience exceeds what you’re paying.”

At a time when many locals have cut down on dining out, Sietsema shares his five favorite dinners in D.C. that go for $25 or less. The list includes a perfect plate of spaghetti and meatballs at Caruso’s Grocery in Hill East and some finger-lickin’ fried chicken at The Hitching Post in Petworth.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch will retire at the end of this year, The Sun’s Torrie Herrington reports. His departure comes after months of criticism from the Trump administration, though he said the White House did not pressure him to leave.

Rise of the machines: Food delivery robots have become increasingly popular in the District, offering contactless delivery from some restaurants in Bloomingdale, Dupont Circle and Logan Circle, The Washington Post reports.

Should D.C. keep its public pools open after Labor Day? At-Large council member Elissa Silverman certainly thinks so. With steamy summer temperatures often extending deep into September, plenty of residents would probably agree. It wouldn’t be a first: Back in 2023, Mayor Muriel Bowser kept two pools and a number of spray parks open past Labor Day, largely due to high temperatures.

City officials say the challenge is both in funding and staffing. Many lifeguards are students who have already returned to school in September. At least our canine friends are set: The annual Doggie Day Swim will take place at four D.C. pools on Saturday.





FROM MARYLAND

Will Jawando, a Montgomery County Council member and the Democratic nominee for county executive, suffered a heart attack Saturday morning during his weekly pickup basketball game, his office said on social media. Jawando is expected to make a full recovery.





FROM VIRGINIA

The Trump administration removed language criticizing a Confederate monument that previously stood at Arlington National Cemetery, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports. The statue is set to be reinstalled next year.





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND

Philadelphia Ballet (5053x2868, AR: 1.76)
For balletomanes: Philadelphia Ballet at Wolf Trap, Thursday.

For “Succession” fans: Brian Cox in “The Score” at Shakespeare Theatre, Friday through Oct. 25.

For something a little different: Adams Morgan Day, Sunday.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

It’s been a long time since Washington has had a franchise quarterback. The Sun’s Thomas Boswell estimates the drought has lasted more than 50 years. But Jayden Daniels has that kind of talent, Boswell writes. So the team’s main objective this season should be pretty simple: Protect him at all costs.

There is no doubt that Daniels is Washington’s most important player. The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson ranked the 10 Commanders who could swing this season, and Daniels was a shoo-in for No. 1. Others on the list: a rookie kicker, an expensive edge rusher and a much-discussed center.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals at Padres, 4:10 p.m. (MLB.TV)

NFL opener: Patriots at Seahawks, 8:20 p.m. (NBC)

Today’s notice: Check out our new duds. Democrats sound the money alarm. OpenAI’s government stake plan may have been a hallucination. And: <Jurassic Park theme music plays.>





THE LATEST

A new Sun over the horizon. What you’re reading right now is the first edition of The Washington Sun’s flagship daily newsletter. What you’re also reading is another edition of the daily newsletter we have been honored to build with you these past couple years. We’re something different today, but also continue to be the thing we hope you’ve come to count on. New name, same great taste.

Why The Sun? Editor-in-Chief Tim Grieve explains: “You can choose your metaphor: We’re shining a light on Washington. Everything is clearer in daylight. And we’d rather light a big candle than keep on cursing the darkness. We cover politics and policy and the people who shape life in Washington — not just at the White House and in Congress, but at the Wilson Building, at Northwest Stadium and in the neighborhoods where we live.”

What this means, by the numbers: We’ve more than doubled the size of our newsroom in just six months, adding top talent up and down the masthead. If you live in the D.C. area or care about people who do, we now have incredible local reporting, restaurant and events coverage, weather forecasts from what used to be called the Capital Weather Gang and more local sports coverage than anyone else in the DMV.

If you live outside the city — or just don’t particularly care if it’s going to rain tomorrow — we have also added top-flight reporters covering national politics and policy, going where the story is and regularly bringing new insights to the conversation.

What it means for you, and us. On our end, we’re very excited for this next chapter. We love good stories as much as you, and there are gonna be a lot more good stories now. On your side of the screen: keep talking to us, telling us what you like and what you don’t. We’re going to be here tomorrow just like always — and you should be, too.

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


Democrats’ money problems: “The money has been slower than anyone anticipated,” Bradley Beychok, co-founder of the Democratic super PAC American Bridge, told The Sun as the fall general-election spending season kicks off in earnest. Our Elena Schneider and Alex Roarty report that outside money groups backing Democrats are desperate for funds, even as polling and other data point to a great environment for their candidates. Just about everyone agrees a blue wave is possible, Elena and Alex write, but no one is sure if Democrats will have the money to help make it happen.





THE BIG ONE

Have AI explain this one to you: For months, OpenAI has been connected to the idea that it’s interested in voluntarily ceding shares to the government. The Sun’s Jeff Stein first broke that story in June.

That was then. Today, Jeff reports OpenAI CEO Sam Altman privately told a group of conservative economists on July 29 that he did not support having the government take shares in the company. To those present, Altman appeared confused why anyone could think he wanted the government to own part of the company.

Altman said that he supports some version of redistributing company shares to the American public, according to multiple sources who attended the event. “I had the sense that he did not see as big of a difference between individual Americans owning shares and the government owning shares as there is in reality,” one attendee said.

What Altman does support: A “government-administered public wealth fund,” which in a statement, OpenAI distinguished from one in which the government took a “controlling or ownership stake in AI companies, which we would not support.” Experts have a hard time understanding exactly what that means, or how it would work.

Today The Washington Sun rises — and with it a belief that we can reimagine the traditional newspaper for the digital age, writes Dana Milbank.

Paleontologists vs. the White House: Donald Trump shrank the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument by more than 90% in July, removing almost 900,000 acres of geologic layers home to unusually complete dinosaur fossils. The move came as a great relief to many Republican lawmakers in Utah, The Sun’s Anna Kramer reports, and a great horror to the state’s dinosaur hunters.

These are some of the world’s greatest dino deposits. The most recent “Jurassic World” featured dinosaurs only known to scientists because of excavations there, Anna writes. But they’re also lands with potentially very valuable minerals underneath that have been locked out of development since the national monument was declared.

In a very deep dive spanning millions of years, Anna carefully scrapes away the politics around dinosaurs, energy extraction and government land protection.

entries.title: Democrats See a Wave. Can They Afford to Ride It?
entries.summary: Democratic strategists say they’re seeing the best polling they’ve ever seen. But “the money is a five-alarm fire.”
entries.content:
Democrats see a wave building. They’ve identified paths to House and Senate majorities that seemed laughable not even a year ago courtesy of an unpopular president, a cost-of-living crisis and a prolonged conflict in Iran.

They also see a potential catastrophic problem in their campaign accounts.

Interviews with two dozen top Democratic and Republican campaign strategists, party officials and donor advisers described an electoral map, eight weeks before Election Day, as teetering between a district-by-district, state-by-state knife fight and a Democratic landslide. But even the most optimistic Democrats said it's not clear they'll have the cash to pull it off.

"The money has been slower than anyone anticipated. It's not at all slow on the candidates’ side, which is maybe the bright spot, but the outside money is not what people expected,” said Bradley Beychok, co-founder of American Bridge, a Democratic super PAC that’s pledged to spend $50 million this cycle. “The money is a five-alarm fire, and the fire starts in September, when the spending gets going, and people are worried."

Mike Smith, who leads the flagship Democratic House super PAC, said, “We all wish that more people were stepping up and doing larger checks. And would that have a material effect on the battlefield? Yes.”

A major Democratic outside group made its own private plea to more than 300 donors and operatives last month. “The next four weeks will determine if we can take advantage of these opportunities, but it requires us to double down on resources now,” according to a copy of the memo, obtained by The Washington Sun.

Those concerns — Republicans swamping Democrats with cash and blunting their momentum this fall — only intensified last week, with the start of spending from Elon Musk and MAGA Inc., where President Donald Trump has $400 million stashed. And even though Democratic candidates have held their own in fundraising against GOP counterparts, Republicans hold a significant combined advantage across outside groups and party committees.

"You can be a shitty candidate and have a shitty campaign and bad environment, and still win by one instead of nine,” said Corry Bliss, a national GOP consultant who led the party’s premier super PAC in 2018. “Of course people are pissed off, but you only have to win by one in these red states,” and red-leaning districts, “so there’s some wiggle room,” he added.

For all the Democratic enthusiasm about expanding their map of targeted races, Republicans started the cycle by shaving down the size of an already shrunken map of competitive seats. The GOP’s historic mid-decade redistricting delivered them a cushion by potentially extracting additional seats from North Carolina, Florida and Texas. The Missouri Supreme Court did grant House Democrats a reprieve last week, denying a Republican effort to eliminate another Democratic incumbent there, though the state has appealed that decision to the Supreme Court.

Both parties agree on the result: The House battlefield is smaller, which will likely yield small margins even if there is a wave, while the Senate map is far larger than either expected last year.

“The president’s job approval is around 38 right now, and that doesn’t bode well for Republicans’ fortunes in the House or the Senate,” said Whit Ayres, a longtime GOP pollster. “In this environment, anything can happen.”

The Democratic case

More than a dozen Democratic strategists and operatives, many of whom were granted anonymity to speak candidly, said this year’s political environment is stronger for their party than it was in 2018.

That belief alone is staggering: The 2018 election was Trump’s first midterm, and his party lost 41 House seats. It’s likely impossible for Democrats to flip that many districts this year given the map, but the party operatives say the backlash to the president is deeper and less ambivalent now than it was then.

Multiple strategists told The Sun that the party’s internal polling in recent months was the best they had ever seen.

“We continue to just get very, very bullish polling results, even out of districts the president won by 12, 13, 14 points,” said one senior Democratic operative, granted anonymity to speak candidly. “It’s really striking.”
House Dems 11/12/25 (7592x5061, AR: 1.50)In Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, for instance, an internal HMP poll obtained by The Sun found that Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures was tied with Republican nominee Rhett Marques, 47% to 47%, despite the fact that Trump won the district by 14 points in 2024.

Another HMP survey obtained by The Sun found the Democratic nominee in Florida’s 22nd Congressional District, Pia Dandiya, leading Republican opponent Casey Askar 46% to 44%. Trump won the district by over 10 points.

Both polls were conducted during the last week of August among likely voters

The surveys are just two of the many internal polls HMP has released in recent months that Republicans dismiss as skewed nonsense but Democrats insist is a genuine reflection of their data.

Party officials say they’re especially heartened by a trend in their internal polling that shows better results in head-to-head matchups with named candidates than in generic ballot tests. They hope that’s proof that most of their candidates can transcend the party’s otherwise dismal image and help it reach further into GOP turf than the national generic ballot suggests is possible.

“We have a bunch of Trump plus 9 to 13 seats. Which of those are gonna come online?” said Smith, HMP’s president. “I think that's a big unknown at this point, but we believe there will be many that do."

The reason the environment is stronger for Democrats now than in 2018 is simple, Democrats say: Trump is less popular overall now than he was then, and voters are less impressed with his management of the economy.

Nationally, Trump’s approval stands at about 38% among adults, according to the Silver Bulletin; exit polls from the 2018 election found his approval rating was at 45% among those who voted.

HMP’s internal polls have found that in the 50 most competitive House districts — where on average Trump won by 5 to 6 points in 2024 —Trump’s approval numbers are underwater on average by 11 points. His statewide numbers are no better: One Democratic strategist familiar with the party’s internal data said the president’s approval is also underwater across Iowa, which has three competitive House races. Trump won the state by 13 points two years ago; he’s now down double digits, the strategist said.

"In 2018, voters didn't like Trump's tweets but they still liked him on the economy,” said Jesse Ferguson, a longtime Democratic strategist. “In 2026, they don't like the tweets or the economy. They're not sold on the Dem brand either — but we spent two years making the case against Republicans and it stuck."

In interviews, top Democratic strategists characterized the map as on the verge of shifting from one contested primarily in purple states and districts to one fought mostly on very red terrain, including Senate races in Kansas and South Carolina.

House operatives touted positive polling in places like Texas 35th Congressional District, a district redrawn last year to be a safe Republican hold, and expressed deep confidence that Democratic nominee Jamie Ager would win North Carolina’s conservative-leaning 11th Congressional District, even after disgraced Republican Rep. Chuck Edwards was forced from the race. They outlined an extensive wish list of the districts they believed could emerge in the race’s final weeks, including Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, Ohio’s 10th and 15th Districts, Kentucky’s 6th District and South Carolina’s 1st District.
Election 2026 House Democrats (4000x2667, AR: 1.50)Except for North Carolina’s 11th District, each of those races is currently rated as likely or solidly Republican by the Cook Political Report.

But even as they say that they’ve laid the groundwork to push deep into Republican territory, party strategists say they aren’t about to start shifting party resources en masse outside their existing core battlefield.

The environment could shift belatedly in Trump’s favor, or a White House that aggressively masterminded a series of redistricting processes could deploy another roadblock for Democrats in the final weeks. And even after extensive efforts to correct their polling after misses in 2016 and 2020, Democrats still have some lingering doubts about their accuracy. The landscape is competitive enough that even a minor misjudgment about the environment could be costly, strategist say

“Some of this stuff comes back and it’s like, what am I to make of a survey showing a lead in a district that Donald Trump won by 15?” said the senior Democratic operative. “Those are real, but doesn’t it make you want to check your math twice?”

And even if their polling is correct at the moment, they worry that Republican-leaning voters will eventually return home to the GOP by Election Day, especially after an expected ad blitz depicting Democratic candidates as radical socialists.

"I think a lot of the paid media kicks off now, and that's where you see vote movement, right?” said Will Van Nuys, the deputy executive director of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. “You see debates and a lot of more oppo and earned media hits. You see a lot more in terms of where money is going, right, and a lot of folks starting to say, ‘OK, are Republicans actually going to keep the House, or are they not?’”

Money remains the biggest stumbling block.

“Us winning a lot of races means winning a lot of races by very small margins,” Smith said. “If you're putting in two, three, four, five million in outside money into one of those places, that can have the impact to sway an election, for sure.”

The Republican case 

Republican strategists know they’ve got the wind in their face. But their path to a better-than-expected November improved over the last year, after banking easy pickups through mid-decade redistricting. To pull it off, more has to break their way: Swamping the other side in campaign spending through the fall; disqualifying Democratic candidates as too crazy; and amping base turnout across the country.

“I can easily paint a picture where this is a state-by-state, district-by-district fight. Or, I can see a picture where Republicans are about to get smoked,” said a national Republican consultant. “The difference between those two pictures is Republican turnout.”

Trump’s promise to return to the campaign trail may be a welcome strategy for some GOP members, particularly those in redder districts. Though others, including some swing seat incumbents, are putting some distance between themselves and the president, including by opting out of appearing at Trump’s midterms convention in Dallas this week.

“We do have an enthusiasm problem, and he’s the only one who can get people to vote, so we need him out there,” said a top Republican strategist who works on congressional races. “We have the money to then go talk to the middle.”

Even some Democrats privately acknowledge that a handful of their candidates will make their jobs harder.

Take Michigan’s 7th District, where a pair of moderate Democratic candidates split the primary vote and set up a win for William Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement. Some Democrats fear Lawrence won’t be able to flip this evenly divided seat. The same is true in Colorado’s 8th District, where state Rep. Manny Rutinel dispatched a more moderate state legislator in his primary. There, too, Democrats privately complain about Rutinel’s progressive track record — he’s “got a lot of baggage,” said a Colorado Democratic strategist.

New Hampshire’s Senate race is also raising concerns for Democratic operatives, two of whom pointed to recent public polling that shows Rep. Chris Pappas trailing Republican John Sununu. The Michigan Senate race is also causing some heartburn for Democrats, as Abdul El-Sayed has stumbled into controversies.
Abdul El-Sayed (4561x3041, AR: 1.50)Republicans say they’ve been preparing since the election cycle began to defy history and hold the House and Senate this year, pouring resources into an all-of-party effort to boost turnout that traditionally sags in midterm elections. Some of them suggested the public boasts from Democrats about expanding the map this fall are more a strategic effort to put Republicans on the defensive, rather than a sincere expression of where they think the election stands.

“There’s a lot more money, in a smaller playing field. That’s why they’re trying to draw us in,” said one senior GOP strategist, who thought Democrats would ultimately spend more defending an incumbent like Rep. Tom Suozzi in New York than in some of the reach districts they say they’re targeting.

In a statement, National Republican Campaign Committee spokesman Mike Marinella reiterated the party’s perceived advantages: “a more favorable map with historic fundraising, stronger candidates, and a commonsense agenda.” Democrats, he said, are meanwhile “saddled with a deeply unpopular agenda and radical socialist nominees hijacking the must-win districts they need to take the majority.”

Nonetheless, Republicans know they’re staring down a tough year. They see that gas is averaging $4.15 a gallon, while diesel climbs even higher. The generic ballot hovers just below a 6-point advantage for Democrats, just a point or two south of what one GOP pollster said would “not be survivable” for his party.

“If you go up to Democrats plus seven, eight, then you can add dozens more seats to the battlefield,” the person added. “I’m glad today isn’t Election Day.”

The battleground map — what is seen as competitive versus what is out of reach — is already showing signs of reshaping. Last week, CLF cut its first offensive target, canceling spending on behalf of state Sen. Peter Oberacker, who is challenging Rep. Josh Riley (D-New York).

entries.title: Rare Coins, State Secrets and Gold Teeth: Inside D.C.’s Lost and Found
entries.summary: A small city government office reunites people with their items — and has more than $760 million in unclaimed money.
entries.content:
Lynn Hall wasn’t having it.

“You cannot go into the vault,” she somewhat sternly told me, shutting down my journalistic impulse to enter any type of room referred to as, well, a vault.

This vault, though, wasn’t full of money, nor was it located in the basement of an ornate bank named after a wealthy owner from yesteryear. Instead, the vault is in an easy-to-miss D.C. government building in Southwest — and it’s packed with people’s stuff.

In official government lingo, it’s unclaimed property. And Lynn Hall is its keeper.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Hall runs the unit within the city’s Office of the Chief Financial Officer that’s responsible for reuniting people with their stuff. Call it D.C.’s municipal version of the lost and found — and it’s not just pennies we’re talking about.

Hall estimates that her office has more than $760 million worth of people’s money in the form of unclaimed refunds, misdelivered paychecks and bank accounts that someone may have just forgotten they had. (You can check if any of it is yours here.)

But the unit also deals in physical belongings. Once a year banks release the contents of safe deposit boxes that are delinquent on rent payments, at which point the city government assumes the responsibility of reuniting the items with their owners or any surviving relatives. Hall’s staff will catalog what comes in, have it formally appraised, and if the original owners or their families can’t be found within a certain time frame, eventually auction it off.
DC0A0776 copy.jpg (9854x4869, AR: 2.02)In most cases it’s jewelry or coins. One recent auction for a $20 gold coin from 1924 started around $2,500 and approached $3,000 toward the end of the 10-day bidding period. A lot of 27 Morgan silver dollar coins, minted in 1883, was set to fetch more than $1,100. A single Confederate $5 bill went for just over $30. An appraiser recently estimated that a gold $20 coin from 1907 could get between $15,000 and $20,000.

The goal isn’t to pad the city’s coffers, though; it’s to set aside the proceeds for any claims that a rightful owner may eventually make. “Every dollar we get, they get,” she says.

And it’s plenty of dollars: Between the checks, refunds and money made from auctions, Hall’s unit returns some $35 million to their owners every year.

Some of the items Hall deals with lean toward the more quixotic. There’s a Vest-Pocket Webster’s Dictionary — “for Constant Use” — from 1899. A bottle of Champagne that can’t be sold (“We don’t have a liquor license,” she says). There’s the occasional gun, knife or illegal drugs. (D.C. police gets those.) Hall once found a diaper, and there have even been locks of hair and umbilical cords.
DC0A1182 copy.jpg (8144x8144, AR: 1.00)“We get teeth all the time,” gold and otherwise, says Blair Spear, an unclaimed property specialist, sounding none too pleased.

The unit will often deal with family keepsakes like military medals, manuscripts, plays, patents for interesting devices and old photos. Those they try to reunite with their owners or any surviving family. And in some cases, what they uncover could well have historic value.

Spear says she once found memos and cables from a former foreign service officer reporting on what he felt was a suspicious dinner in Mexico between a group of Cubans and Lee Harvey Oswald, who later assassinated President John F. Kennedy. Spear says she’s working with the officer's daughter to return the papers. (Where that’s not possible, they reach out to museums to gauge interest; they often don’t get responses.)

In another case, Spear found savings bonds in one of the abandoned safe deposit boxes that belonged to a woman who had died and was survived by a son. “He had no idea they existed,” she says. “So he got a letter in the mail that resulted in $18,000 in bonds.”
DC0A1279 copy.jpg (6553x3247, AR: 2.02)Hall has been in unclaimed property since 1989, first for Maryland before coming to D.C. in 2013. In that time she’s seen a significant drop in the number of safe deposit boxes her unit gets on an annual basis, from what used to be 1,000 a year to maybe 100 now. “The safe deposit boxes are becoming more obsolete,” she concedes.

Still, her team isn’t about to run out of property to auction and items to reunite with their owners. The vault — the one she banned me from entering — remains full. And that, adds Hall, keeps the job interesting.

“That’s the great thing about unclaimed property,” she says. “Every day is different.”

entries.title: Tom Sietsema's 5 Favorite Dinners in D.C. for $25 (or Less!)
entries.summary: These five D.C. restaurants, easy on the budget, spark joy in different ways.
entries.content:
Few of us are immune to the soaring cost of just about everything these days. One life pleasure I refuse to give up is dining out.

To make it work, I look less for inexpensive restaurants, period, and more for places where the experience exceeds what you’re paying. The following five D.C. restaurants, easy on the budget, spark joy in different ways. Each also offers a gently priced main course or more that makes it easy for you to become a regular.

Caruso’s Grocery

I can’t recall the last time I booked a table here. Reservations for prime times are in such demand, I simply show up when the doors open and grab one of eight stools at the softly lit bar of one of the coziest restaurants I know.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Just about everything you order in this Italian American charmer from chef Matt Adler is a model of what it should be. Calamari gets sprinkled with semolina and fried so parts are crisp and parts are soft. A salad of bitter radicchio, endive, juicy citrus and saline green olives makes a perfect segue to one of the hearty main courses, like chicken parm or veal francaise. Be sure to check out the seasonal specials, which recently scattered tender shrimp and crisp corn on a bed of fusilli, everything draped with carbonara sauce. Each bite seemed to include a silky bit of smoked pancetta.

The steal, though, is spaghetti and meatballs for just under $25. The pasta is made in house and shows nice resistance; the meatballs seem to be shaped primarily from pork and heat. A server asks if you want cheese, and you nod. Onto the surface go snowy filings of Parmesan. Caruso’s Grocery offers gratis bread to start. Crusty slices from Uptown Bakery make a great sop for any remaining tomato sauce.

The restaurant, in the Hill East neighborhood, is dressed to look the part of an old-time Italian joint while nodding to two of co-founder Michael Babin’s Sicilian great uncles, who opened a market in Baton Rouge in 1920. Diners are shown to marinara-colored banquettes, walls display albums’ worth of black-and-white photographs, and in keeping with the “grocery” theme, bottles of wine and more are stacked on high shelves. With the check come peppermint candies, another sweet touch in a place packed with them.

1401 Pennsylvania Ave. SE
202-661-0148
carusosgrocery.com
(The younger Maryland branch is at 11820 Trade St. in North Bethesda.) 

Chercher Ethiopian Restaurant

When I crave a little quiet, you’ll find me on the tiny rear patio, crawling with vines and watched over by the attentive staff of one of the city’s prized sources for Ethiopian. Sometimes, I spring for doro wot, the slow-cooked, chicken-and-egg stew that’s considered Ethiopia’s national treasure. Often, I find space for kitfo, the lush, tongue-tingling minced sirloin that fans know is best eaten raw and leaves a trail of fire, from the spice blend mitmita, in its wake.

Always, I order the vegan deluxe sampler ($23), 10 meatless stews and salads whose colors create a rainbow coalition on a platter lined with injera, the tangy, spongy bread that doubles as a utensil. A trio of lentil stews — some a touch sweet, some a lot spicy— top the edible canvas, along with shimmering diced beets, garlic-laced collard greens, porridge-like orange shiro and turmeric-tinted cabbage and carrots, lightly cooked to retain some bite. (“We don’t kill the cabbage,” owner Alemayehu Abebe likes to say.) Did I forget to mention wizened green beans in a tangle of onions? The spread is a lot to take in, and a lot to enjoy.

There are three Chercher locations. The original in Shaw, my favorite, opened in 2012 and finds 100 seats across three levels. A storefront on 14th Street Northwest claims the largest kitchen and is where the bulk of the stews and injera are made, then transferred via van to the other branches. Hence the consistency from branch to branch, a detail underscored by Abebe, who says he tastes everything so the food is “always the same.”

Call me a cheerleader. When travel gurus Rick Steves and Samantha Brown came to D.C., Chercher is where I broke bread — well, injera — with them.

1334 9th St. NW
202-299-9703
chercherrestaurant.com
(The other branches are at 3608 14th St. NW and 4921 Bethesda Ave., Bethesda.)

The Hitching Post

Al and Adrienne Carter introduced the soul food purveyor in Petworth in 1967. Barry Dindyal, a native of Guyana, bought The Hitching Post from the couple 45 years later. Wisely, while adding a few dishes of his own, Dindyal kept the bulk of the Carters’ recipes.

I drop by frequently, not just for the consistent cooking (the peerless fried whiting is seasoned like always with dried garlic and paprika), but for the sense of community. I never go that I don’t run into public radio star Kojo Nnamdi, who is such a regular that he has a drink named for him.
Hitching Post (7131x4754, AR: 1.50)More often than not these days, I gravitate to Dindyal’s fried chicken ($25), which is bought fresh, cut up in the kitchen, dipped in an egg wash and dredged in flour seasoned with garlic, paprika, black pepper and dried thyme. The entree is cooked to order, so be patient, because 20 minutes of waiting rewards diners with fabulous, finger-licking-good, Sunday supper eating. The crisp-golden skin barely clings to four moist pieces of chicken, and the price includes a choice of two homey side dishes. The creamy potato salad, punctuated with sweet pickle relish and boosted with dry mustard and celery seeds, is usually part of my plate, as are collard greens, which are pleasing (and vegan) with oregano, allspice and garlic.

Fun fact: The Carters live above the restaurant, and Adrienne sometimes comes down for whole fish. More frequently, says Dindyal, he walks upstairs for a visit with “a beer or two” in hand.

200 Upshur St. NW
202-726-1511
thehpostrestaurant.com 

Donsak Thai Restaurant 

This slip of a Thai eatery in Woodley Park gives us so many reasons to make it a habit. The vast list, 75 dishes long, flags items that are vegan or gluten- and peanut-free, and devotes a section to the distinct heat and funk of Essan, the cuisine of Thailand’s northeastern region. If you live within 1.5 miles, delivery is free with a $25 minimum. It’s named for Don Sak, a district in southern Thailand known for its seafood — and the birthplace of co-owner Supisa “Boom” Teawbut — and the dining room reinforces the water theme with navy blue banquettes.

Best of all for bargain hunters, one of the least-expensive selections is also one of the kitchen’s best: green curry ($17), its velvety coconut milk base sparked and stained with green chiles and cilantro and chock-full of vegetables (eggplant, bell pepper, bamboo) that are lightly steamed before being introduced to the bowl. The seductive aroma comes from the inclusion of dried lime leaf peel, which Teawbut brings back from Thailand when she visits. Optional toppings include beef, pork, more vegetables, tofu and my go-to steamed chicken, served in generous ivory folds. A small bowl of warm rice rounds out the pleasure.

Donsak, illuminated by a front window and a skylight over the rear bar, gained a sibling when a larger branch with the same name rolled out in Georgetown in July. While the menus are similar, having tasted both, my affection remains with the original.

2608 Connecticut Ave. NW
202-507-8207
donsakthai.com
(The Georgetown branch is at 3251 Prospect St. NW.)

Her Diner 

Watching our server navigate our cocktail order from bar to booth involves an impressive balancing act. The drinks are big and served to the brim, yet not a drop of margarita or Manhattan is lost. Better yet, both libations taste as if they were shaken and stirred in a far fancier establishment.

Her Diner is the chapter following Duplex Diner, the longtime Adams Morgan hangout popular with the LGBTQ community, whose general manager, Kelly Laczko, took over and refreshed the space a couple of years ago. Customers stroll into the bi-level space — a bar and a sunken dining room with concrete floors and Crayola colors here and there — and peruse plastic menus that tap into nostalgia. Salisbury steak? Chicken pot pie? This son of the Midwest laughed at the sight of “totchos,” a sharable appetizer pairing tater tots with spicy ground beef, queso, jalapeños and ranch sour cream dressing. Sure sounds like a Mexican-themed hot dish to me!

Comparisons to the long-lived, gay-friendly Annie’s Paramount Steak House in Dupont Circle are inevitable. I’d say the service is better at Annie’s — entrees and appetizers came together at Her Diner — and the food is a few notches higher at Her Diner. I’m a sucker for meatloaf ($20). Her Diner serves a crusty slab of meat that a server tells us uses Salisbury steak. The entree gets topped with a chunky tomato sauce and flanked with homey mashed potatoes and bright green beans, for a dish that tastes like a mom might be in the kitchen. (Not to worry if you don’t eat meat. For two bucks more, there’s meatloaf made with Impossible burger.)

A runner-up to my No. 1 pick is the packed-with-chicken pot pie ($22), filled with bright carrots and soft mushrooms in a light sauce to bind everything. The puff pastry dome is a nice touch, but it always needs to be baked longer.

2004 18th St. NW
202-204-1761
herdiner.com

entries.title: Ranking the 10 Most Important Commanders Ahead of the 2026 Season
entries.summary: From a rookie kicker to the franchise quarterback, these players will need to produce.
entries.content:
Around this time last season, vibes were high in D.C. The Commanders were coming off an impromptu trip to the NFC championship game, and it seemed like the stench of the previous 25 years had finally been fumigated.

But things fell apart quickly. The team won seven less games than it did in 2024, Jayden Daniels spent more time on the bench than he did under center and several players who were supposed to be difference-makers turned out to be nonfactors.

With a new NFL season kicking off today, let’s look at the players who will shape this year in Washington. If everything goes right with this group of 10, there’s a chance the Commanders can make it one game further than they did in 2024. If not, this fall could be a sequel to 2025.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

10. Drew Stevens

Here’s some trivia for you: How many kickers have attempted at least one field goal for the Commanders since the 2016 season? The answer: 11.

Washington’s kicking game has been so inconsistent that in two of those seasons (2021 and 2024) it used four kickers. After a camp battle with incumbent veteran Jake Moody, the Commanders are hoping Stevens, a rookie out of Iowa, is the answer.

He was consistent throughout camp and connected from 60-plus yards on multiple occasions. For a team that finished 8-5 in one-score games two years ago and 2–5 in those contests last year, having a reliable kicker is of the utmost importance.

9. Sonny Styles

Last season the Commanders missed the second-most tackles (131) in the NFL, according to Pro Football Reference. Washington also allowed the third-most rushing yards.

Washington is banking on Styles, who totaled 182 tackles and 17 tackles for loss his final two seasons at Ohio State, to shore up those areas. The No. 7 overall pick brings exceptional quickness and instincts to the linebacker position, in part because he used to play safety. While few of those traits stood out in limited snaps across two preseason games, Styles has played well in practice, showing an ability to hit running gaps with speed and blow up plays before they have a chance to start.

Bill Croskey-Merritt AP - 25278805543622 (4359x2906, AR: 1.50)
8. Bill Croskey-Merritt

There’s no doubt the Commanders offense runs through Daniels, but if the quarterback has any shot at recapturing his magic from 2024, he’ll need help from his lead running back. Offensive coordinator David Blough’s system will lean heavily on play-action and bootlegs, and those play calls only work if there’s a dependable run game.

Croskey-Merritt showed flashes of his light feet, speed and power last season, particularly against the Chargers in Week 5 (16 touches for 150 yards and two touchdowns), but lacked consistency. His offseason dedication to conditioning and pass-catching has impressed the coaching staff, but time will tell if he can be a reliable, every-down back.

7. Terry McLaurin

There are few Commanders more eager to not talk about last season than McLaurin. After five straight 1,000-yard seasons, the wide receiver finished 2025 with career lows in receptions (38), yards (582) and touchdowns (3). That was due in part to a training camp holdout and a quad injury that limited him to 10 games, a career low.

Based on the explosive plays he’s made through training camp, McLaurin looks like his normal self this year. Plus, the arrival of Stefon Diggs means he doesn’t have to carry the receivers room on his back anymore.

6. Nick Allegretti

Throughout training camp, Washington’s interior offensive line struggled to give Daniels and company enough time to make plays. And it wasn’t just on pass plays: Commanders running backs averaged 3.6 yards per carry this preseason, which would have tied for last in the league in 2025.

Coach Dan Quinn and general manager Adam Peters have stressed all offseason that Allegretti, the team’s presumed starter at center, is the answer to these problems. The only issue is that Allegretti only practiced a handful of times during camp. If Allegretti, who has only 178 career snaps at center in the NFL, isn’t the answer then the Washington offense will struggle to reach its potential.

5. Stefon Diggs

If Diggs lives up to his own statement that he is the league’s best No. 2 receiver, then the Commanders’ passing attack will be unlike anything we’ve seen in years. Washington has long needed someone opposite McLaurin who can reliably beat coverage and make tough catches, and Diggs has proven that throughout his 12-year career.

Whether lining up in the slot or on the outside, Diggs has proven to be a reliable safety valve for every quarterback he’s played with. He and Daniels formed an immediate connection in training camp despite Diggs showing up on Aug. 7.

4. Amik Robertson

While the Commanders’ defensive production will be heavily dependent on the front seven (more below), they will need above-average play from their defensive backs. Defensive coordinator Daronte Jones comes from a Vikings team that had the highest blitz rate (48%) and eighth-highest zone coverage rate (77.1%) last season, according to Sharp Football Analysis.

This means that if the pass rush doesn’t get to the quarterback, then the defensive backs will be stuck covering large swaths of field for long periods of time. With incumbent starter Trey Amos out with an ankle injury for at least the first four games of the season, Washington will depend heavily on Robertson, who mostly lined up on the outside in camp, and the rest of the defensive backs to hold up in coverage.

The only issue? Robertson allowed the third-most passing yards (808) in coverage last year with the Lions, according to Next Gen Stats. (Washington’s Mike Sainristil ranked fifth.)

Robertson has shown the ability to provide sticky coverage and blow up plays, but without a better showing from him this year, Commanders will finish near the bottom of the league in passing yards allowed for a second straight season.

Odafe Oweh AP - 25323687165192 (6602x4401, AR: 1.50)
3. Odafe Oweh

All that being said, Robertson and company may not have to hold their coverage for that long.

The Commanders completely retooled their front seven this offseason, bringing in rookie Styles and free agents Tim Settle, K’Lavon Chaisson and Oweh to shore up a unit that forced the seventh-fewest pressures (121) despite tying for the eighth-most sacks (42) in 2025.

Oweh, who spent last season with the Ravens and Chargers, was an unstoppable force throughout camp, mucking up nearly every play he was on the field for. Last season he was the second-best edge rusher behind only Micah Parsons, according to ESPN’s pass rush win rate formula. If opposing quarterbacks have to worry about Oweh getting to them this season, that opens up opportunities for the 10 other defenders to make a game-changing play.

2. Brandon Coleman

The interior offensive line has rightfully borne the brunt of the criticism this offseason, but Coleman is the most important member of the unit. After Washington lost starting left tackle Laremy Tunsil, Coleman was thrust back into the role he played as a rookie in 2024.

There’s no replacing a five-time Pro Bowler like Tunsil, but Coleman has done his best impression since taking over in early August. He’s held his own in practice against the Commanders edge rushers and in the three snaps he saw in the preseason against Detroit. Washington is hoping he can keep that form as the season gets going.

1. Jayden Daniels

No surprise here. The main difference between an NFC championship game appearance in 2024 and a 5-12 flameout last fall was Daniels’ availability. He started and finished just four games last season compared to 15 games the year before.

When Daniels is on the field, he’s one of the most electric players in all of football. As a rookie, he ranked sixth in completion percentage (69%) and 10th in passing touchdowns (25) while also ranking second among quarterbacks in rushing yards (891). His 64 rushing first downs ranked 10th among all rushers.

Under Blough, Daniels is expected to play more under center, use more huddles and be allowed to make more decisions at the line. The hope is that this will keep the defense guessing and lead to more explosive plays.

But if the offensive line can’t hold up, or Daniels continues to take the hits that caused him to miss 10 games last year, it won’t really matter how well Coleman or Oweh or Diggs performs. The Commanders will only go as far as Daniels takes them.
entries.author: Martenzie Johnson

entries.title: This Commanders Season Is About One Thing: Saving Jayden Daniels
entries.summary: D.C. hasn’t had a franchise quarterback in more than 50 years. For Daniels to get there, he first needs to survive.
entries.content:
Save Jayden Daniels.

That is all that the Washington Commanders season should be about.

You can develop young players, master new systems and win when you can. That will help for years. But not if JD5 becomes RGIV.

From the top down, but especially with new offensive coordinator David Blough and Daniels himself, the imperative must be to maximize the chance that Daniels will still be the team’s QB1 — and a better, more developed quarterback — in ’30. And ’35, when he'll still only be 34.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Deferred gratification tastes bitter. This season is spinach so that the next 10 years can be, mostly, cake and ice cream.

Washington hasn’t had a quarterback with “franchise” level talent in over 50 years. Despite a step backward in every metric in ’25, Daniels still has it — if he survives to develop it fully.

Even when things look bleak, you may get a lucky break in the midst of the mess. That good fortune for Washington is the arrival of Blough.
David Blough (4838x3226, AR: 1.50)His system, largely learned from Ben Johnson in Detroit and Kevin O’Connell in Minnesota, uses every NFL theory that preserves the health and maximizes the weapons of a star quarterback over a long career.

By no coincidence whatsoever, Blough replaces his style-box antithesis, sugar-high coordinator Kliff Kingsbury — thanks for ’24, Kliff! — and his college-style spread offense. Unfortunately, the Kingsbury shotgun often seemed aimed at the slender Daniels’ head.

In ’24, Daniels escaped, brilliantly, despite three games in which he carried the ball 16 times. In ’25, Daniels led NFL QBs in carries per game (8.3). But there were only seven such games because he was hurt four times.

His knee was sprained while scrambling between the tackles in a blowout loss to Green Bay. His left elbow was gruesomely dislocated, bent completely the wrong way like a hinged toy, when he was asked to run near the goal line with the team down 38-7. Narrow the score so the coaches don’t look so bad? Two weeks later — sickeningly — he was back. And blasted again.

Suddenly, everybody got it: Save Jayden Daniels.

Now, we’ll find out: Can they?

Before their opener Sunday against the Eagles in Philly, the Commanders have headaches. The defense, which couldn’t stop anybody last season (last in yards allowed), is dealing with injury issues.

The offense, which added free agent wide receiver Stefon Diggs to complement Terry McLaurin, now has an offensive line in total flux. "Flux" being the technical term for OMG!

The great left tackle Laremy Tunsil, Daniels’ blind side protector, will miss most, if not all of the season with a torn triceps. After the team released solid center Tyler Biadasz in February, presumably to save salary cap space, it is now almost naked at the position. Will ex-guard Nick Allegretti, out for weeks this summer with a calf injury, be ready for Philly? Maybe. Otherwise, a sixth-round rookie will start at center. Light a candle.

The starting O-line on the depth chart has had z-e-r-o reps together — ever.

Fortunately, time passes. Injuries heal. On a team that won only five games last year and is predicted to win seven in ’26, the proper view is the long view. That’s why I can’t wait to see if Daniels adapts, grows and, in time, flourishes in a Blough system that looks heaven-sent for him.

It’ll take time. But, with Daniels in the Blough system, what should we look for?

In recent years, the NFL has trended toward running more plays with the quarterback under center. The leaders last year were the Rams (60% ), the champion Seahawks (55), Bills (51), Lions (49) and Bears (49). Lots of success there.

In ’25, Daniels ran only 5.8% of plays under center. Look for an eight-times increase?

Why go under center? Because, since the T-formation was born, the run game works better that way; it’s more deceptive and versatile. On the handoff, or fake, the QB’s back is to the defense, his body deliberately blocking their view of the ball. (Daniels’ crafty temperament should love the upgrade from the pro-forma fakes in the gun to the hard fakes of a dedicated ball-handling magician under center.)

For a split second, nobody knows who has it. Linebackers hesitate. Defensive backs have a harder read, too, and are more vulnerable to deep play-action passes. Blocking angles and ability to run “outside zone” plays are better. (You don’t need to take it from me, a mediocre ex-high school QB during the Mesozoic era; there are whole books on this.)

Star coaches Sean McVay, Kyle Shanahan and Johnson all preach this sermon as the NFL becomes a more run-centric league. In ’25, 17 players rushed for 1,000 yards. In ’15, it was seven.

The better you run the ball, the more you neutralize the defense’s pass rush. Play action also opens up rollouts, which get a mobile passer like Daniels away from traffic, and violence. If he’s willing to focus downfield on the throw, rather than the brave gain-a-few run which too often tempts him, it’s win-win.

Blough also prefers to huddle up, not play fast-break style. Kingsbury’s idea was to play so fast that defenses couldn’t change personnel packages, or call complex pressures as much as they liked. This made the QB’s job of defense recognition easier. But the spread is also a more predictable offense with fewer ways to do what Blough loves: “Spread the field horizontally and vertically.” (Oh, no, more X-and-O books.)

However, when you huddle, the defense can organize itself to call any complex lying, shifting picture that it wants before the snap; so, as Daniels turns his back to handoff, fake or drop back, by the time he turns around he may see a horrifyingly different defensive look.

Being under center helps you deceive them. But it can help them deceive you, too.

From new footwork to reading through a “pure progression” passing game like Blough’s, where you sift through your receivers in a predetermined order, Daniels has work to do. That’s understandable; even though everyone who’s coached Daniels raves about his high football IQ, it’s tough to ask a rookie to have a PhD in reading NFL defenses. But this is Daniels’ third year. He should be on schedule, maybe not early in ’26, but over time — or whenever he finally has a functional O-line — to prove that he’s a studious, observant quarterback who wins the brain game. Under Blough, Daniels will also have more control at the line to get out of “bad plays” before the snap and get swamped-and-stomped less often.

That doesn’t mean the Commanders will completely discard favorite Daniels plays from the past. You haven't seen the last read option. But, as Daniels told The Athletic last week, “Let’s [just] say there will be less designed quarterback runs.” (If there aren’t, after ’25, someone should be fired.)
Jayden Daniels Seahawks (5915x3944, AR: 1.50)But the final, and biggest piece of the “Save Jayden Daniels” puzzle is Daniels himself. He has shown little inclination to stay behind the line, looking to pass, once he has scrambled successfully and established a “second pocket.” He ran more and passed less (39%) than any QB in scramble situations last year. Only two others were barely under 50%. Most learn, “Look long, look medium, throw it away.”

From a child, Daniels has made Superman Plays. They draw awe, not just success. Is that showmanship, leadership and pride so deep in his personality that he can't or won't change it?

Daniels needs models. Whether it’s Patrick Mahomes, or prime Aaron Rodgers, or long-ago Roger Staubach, there have been Hall of Fame quarterbacks who scrambled all over the field. But most were waiting for a big play to open up down the field, not for a chance to gain 10 yards and get blown up. Roger The Dodger averaged 3.1 runs per game. From age 26 to 33, Rodgers averaged 3.6 runs. For Mahomes, 3.9 a game.

If it’s enough for them, it ought to be for Daniels. You don’t run when a first down is on the line. You run when the game is on the line.

The NFL is human demolition derby. Switching to a less self-destructive offense improves your odds. Nothing makes you safe. Until the line is functional, which may not be until Tunsil is back, Daniels will be tempted to “save the day.” So, go on and worry.

As always, at least for the last 57 years since Vince Lombardi came to D.C. to coach, fans of the Commanders are insanely optimistic. If the experts say “seven wins,” then they start counting at 10. You can’t tell ’em anything, bless their hearts. Often, they even refuse to believe a whole season’s worth of final scores.

Everybody, including Daniels, needs a serving of reality and deferred gratification. No one will remember whether Washington won the Super Bowl this year, because they won’t.

But we’ll remember whether Jayden Daniels survived and if he improved. That “scoreboard” will impact the next decade.
